key_insight: Multi-agent systems are not universally better than single-agent systems; their advantage depends on how information is shared and compressed across agents. From an information bottleneck view, MAS can help when they reduce overload and preserve the right reasoning signals, but can hurt when they lose critical context through fragmentation.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the unclear and inconsistent performance gap between LLM-based multi-agent systems and single-agent systems on complex tasks, explaining when and why MAS actually provides a benefit.
method: Reframes MAS vs. SAS through an information bottleneck perspective on reasoning and context flow.
Compares how a single agent stores the full reasoning trace in one shared context versus multiple agents operating with isolated local contexts.
Analyzes how communication constraints and context partitioning affect information retention, reasoning quality, and final task performance.
impact: For AI practitioners, this work offers a principled way to decide whether to use a multi-agent design instead of assuming it will improve performance. It can guide better system architecture choices for tasks that are reasoning-heavy, communication-limited, or prone to context overload.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram of SAS vs. MAS context flow
Information bottleneck pipeline showing input, compression, communication, and output
Trade-off chart comparing context overload vs. information loss
Icons for agents, shared memory, and message passing
paper_title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
paper_authors: Wendi Yu, Lianhao Zhou, Xiangjue Dong, Sai Sudarshan Barath, Declan Staunton
